title: Narrative Versus Reason-Based Messages to Promote Prostate Cancer Screening Among Black Men: A Randomized Experiment
content: Background/Objectives: Black men in the United States have the highest prostate cancer incidence and approximately twice the mortality of White men. Health communication is one modifiable contributor to disparities in early detection, alongside structural and health-system determinants. This study tested whether narrative messaging outperforms reason-based messaging in shaping affect toward screening and intention to discuss screening with a physician among Black men who reported no prior prostate cancer screening. Methods: In a three-arm randomized experiment, 268 Black men aged ≥40 years were assigned to a reason-based brochure (n = 91), a narrative brochure featuring a survivor’s story (n = 80), or a minimal control brochure (n = 97). Condition effects were estimated with analyses of covariance adjusted for demographic characteristics; differences by subgroup and belief level were examined in exploratory interaction models. Results: Narrative messaging did not outperform reason-based messaging on affect toward screening (F(2, 250) = 1.58, p = .207) or screening intention (F(2, 250) = 1.67, p = .190). In exploratory analyses, condition effects on intention differed by ethnicity (African American vs. other Black men; F(2, 248) = 5.96, p = .003) and by attitude toward prostate cancer detection and prevention (F(2, 247) = 8.28, p < .001); among men with less favorable post-exposure attitudes, the narrative brochure was associated with higher intention than the control brochure (difference = 0.61, p < .001). Both message brochures were rated as more engaging than the control brochure (F(2, 249) = 4.93, p = .008). Attitude, perceived behavioral control, cultural orientation, and fatalism were associated with intention. Conclusions: No single message format was superior overall. Narrative messages may warrant further study among less receptive men, and messages that address attitudes and beliefs may matter more than format alone.
